repos.name: alibaba / open-code-review
repos.description: Fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.

summary.goal: Open Code Review (OCR) is an AI-powered code review CLI tool, originally built internally at Alibaba Group, that reads Git diffs, sends changed files to a configurable LLM via a tool-using agent, and produces structured, line-level review comments. Beyond diffs, `ocr scan` reviews whole files for auditing codebases with no meaningful diff. More details: https://open-codereview.ai.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review`, then configure a provider and model via `ocr config provider` and `ocr config model` (skippable in Delegation Mode). Run `ocr review` for workspace, branch-range, or commit reviews, or `ocr scan` to review whole files/directories without git history; output can be saved as JSON.
summary.pros: Per the documented benchmark (50 repositories, 200 pull requests, 10 languages, 1,505 annotated ground-truth issues), Open Code Review reports significantly higher Precision and F1 than general-purpose agents like Claude Code on the same model, while using only about ~1/9 of the tokens and finishing faster.
summary.cons: The same benchmark documentation states Recall is lower than general-purpose agents, a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise, implying some real defects may be missed.
summary.fit: It requires Git >= 2.41 and, outside Delegation Mode, a configured LLM provider; it seems best suited for teams reviewing diffs, PRs, or unfamiliar codebases, with integrations for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Kimi Code, and CI/CD pipelines.

repos.name: cloudflare / security-audit-skill
repos.description: A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings

summary.goal: This is a coding-agent skill that turns an agent into a security auditor, running a structured six-phase audit: reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting. It originated as the single-repo starting point for Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness.
summary.usage: Install with the Skills CLI: `npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill --skill security-audit` (add `--global` for a user-level install). Then start a coding agent in the target codebase and issue a request such as `security audit this codebase`; matching triggers activate full audit mode, writing reports to `~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>` by default.
summary.pros: Findings undergo adversarial validation, since the agent that checks a candidate is never the one that found it, and reports distinguish confirmed, needs_validation, and rejected verdicts. The findings and coverage-ledger validators are zero-dependency Node scripts. Documentation suggests that in test runs, repeated runs found roughly double the vulnerabilities a single run found.
summary.cons: The workflow requires Node.js for its validators and an OS-enforced sandbox that disables external networking, uses a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforces resource limits, and restricts writes to scratch paths for any target-controlled execution. Without such a sandbox, leads that need code execution remain marked needs_validation rather than being confirmed.
summary.fit: It is intended for coding agents whose underlying model supports tool use and parallel sub-agents, run against a codebase the user points it at. Multiple runs against the same repository are additive, reusing prior ledgers and findings to target coverage gaps rather than repeating prior work.

repos.name: addyosmani / agent-skills
repos.description: Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents.

summary.goal: Agent Skills is a collection of 25 structured engineering workflows ('skills') plus 9 slash commands (/spec, /plan, /build, /test, /constraints, /review, /webperf, /code-simplify, /ship) that guide AI coding agents through spec-writing, planning, implementation, testing, review, and shipping, encoding practices senior engineers use in production software.
summary.usage: Install every skill into 70+ supported agents with `npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills`, or add it as a Claude Code plugin by running `/plugin marketplace add addyosmani/agent-skills` followed by `/plugin install agent-skills@addy-agent-skills`; individual skills can also be installed separately.
summary.pros: Skills activate automatically based on the task at hand, and the `/build auto` command can generate a plan and implement every task in one approved pass while still requiring tests and per-task commits; the pack works across many agent tools and is MIT licensed.
summary.cons: Installing a single skill with npx copies only that skill's folder, not the shared `references/` directory, so supplementary checklists that skill references become unavailable unless the whole repo is used instead. This portability gap is tracked as an open issue (#361).
summary.fit: This project appears suited to teams that want AI coding agents to follow consistent, verifiable engineering discipline (specs, tests, reviews) across tools like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Copilot, and may be especially useful in the Claude Code integration the README recommends.

repos.name: Tencent / BrowserSkill
repos.description: Let AI agents use your real, logged-in browser without interrupting your work. CLI + extension for browser automation across any shell-capable AI agent.

summary.goal: BrowserSkill connects AI coding agents such as Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, Pi, Hermes Agent, and DeepSeek Harness to a browser you are already logged into. An agent must explicitly borrow an open tab, complete its task, and return it, leaving the rest of the browser untouched.
summary.usage: Setup can be delegated to a shell-capable agent using a one-line instruction referencing https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Tencent/BrowserSkill/main/AGENT_INSTALL.md. Manual installation runs `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Tencent/BrowserSkill/main/install.sh | sh` (or install.ps1 on Windows), then verifies with `bsk --version`, adds the Chrome or Microsoft Edge extension, installs the skill with `bsk install-skill`, checks the connection with `bsk doctor`, and starts tasks via `bsk session start`. Updates use `bsk update --yes`.
summary.pros: Agents can reuse existing signed-in sessions instead of separate test accounts, browser tasks run in a visible, separate Agent Window so normal browsing continues, any shell-capable agent can use the bsk CLI without framework lock-in, and built-in human-in-loop handling lets the agent request help for captchas or logins.
summary.cons: Upgrading to version 0.3.0 changed the CLI so that `--unattended`, `tab borrow --no-confirm`, and `BSK_REQUEST_HELP=off` no longer bypass confirmation or disable help requests; equivalent behavior now must be set through the browser extension's automation settings instead. The tool also requires two local runtime pieces (a CLI/daemon plus a browser extension), and Firefox support is currently only planned, not available.
summary.fit: The project fits developers and teams building shell-based AI agent harnesses that need controlled, human-supervised browser automation, including sandboxed or remote setups with configurable tab-borrow and help-request confirmations. Its Cargo/pnpm workspace layout with CLI, protocol, extension, UI/i18n, and evaluation packages suggests an actively maintained, extensible platform.

repos.name: alphaXiv / OpenResearch
repos.description: Turn your coding agents into research agents

summary.goal: OpenResearch is presented as a local-first workspace for research agents and autoresearch, intended to turn coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor into research agents that can review literature, develop hypotheses, run experiments, and produce research artifacts.
summary.usage: It is installed on macOS or Linux with `curl -LsSf https://openresearch.sh/install.sh | sh` followed by `orx up`, which opens a local dashboard at `http://127.0.0.1:4791`. `orx install-skills` adds the OpenResearch skill to supported agents, and `orx up --remote user@host` runs the workspace against remote GPUs while using a local browser.
summary.pros: The README describes parallel exploration through independent agent sessions with isolated git worktrees, reproducible experiments tracked in a git-native tree with an immutable archive per run, and local ownership of projects, logs, and artifacts, alongside a choice of agent and compute backend (local, own infrastructure, or managed OpenResearch compute).
summary.cons: In remote mode over SSH, the documentation states the remote service binds to loopback but has no application-level authentication, so other users on that host can reach it; Windows support is also described as beta and requires Git for Windows.
summary.fit: Given its command-line installation and dependence on external coding agents, it seems best suited for developers or researchers already using tools like Claude Code or Cursor who want git-based experiment tracking, though the remote-access caveat suggests added care on shared hosts.

repos.name: anthropics / claude-code
repos.description: Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that lives in your terminal, understands your codebase, and helps you code faster by executing routine tasks, explaining complex code, and handling git workflows - all through natural language commands.

summary.goal: Claude Code is presented as an agentic coding tool that lives in the terminal, understands a codebase, and helps developers work faster by executing routine tasks, explaining complex code, and handling git workflows through natural language commands. It can also be used inside an IDE or invoked on GitHub via @claude.
summary.usage: The README's recommended install method runs `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS/Linux (or `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows), with Homebrew and WinGet also listed. After installing, users navigate to a project directory and run `claude` to start.
summary.pros: Documented strengths include natural-language handling of git workflows, code explanation, and routine task execution, plus flexibility across terminal, IDE, and GitHub (@claude) contexts. The repository also bundles several plugins that extend functionality with custom commands and agents.
summary.cons: The README marks npm installation (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`) as deprecated in favor of the curl/PowerShell/Homebrew/WinGet methods, so existing npm-based setups may need migration. Node.js 18+ appears required per the repository badge, though this is not restated in the running text.
summary.fit: Given its terminal-based, natural-language design and Node.js 18+ badge, Claude Code appears best suited to developers comfortable working from a command line or IDE who want git and coding-task assistance; teams should also note the feedback-based data collection (via `/bug` and usage data) described in the data policy section.

repos.name: NationalSecurityAgency / ghidra
repos.description: Ghidra is a software reverse engineering (SRE) framework

summary.goal: Ghidra is a software reverse engineering (SRE) framework created and maintained by the National Security Agency (NSA) Research Directorate. It provides tools for disassembly, assembly, decompilation, graphing, and scripting of compiled code, supporting a wide variety of processor instruction sets and executable formats on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
summary.usage: To install, download a Ghidra release, install JDK 25 64-bit, extract the archive, and launch it with `./ghidraRun` (`ghidraRun.bat` on Windows). To build from source, clone the repository with `git clone https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra.git`, install build tools (JDK 25, Gradle 9.1.0+, Python3 3.9-3.14), and run `gradle buildGhidra`.
summary.pros: Ghidra supports both user-interactive and automated analysis modes and can be extended through custom scripts and extensions written in Java or Python. It works across multiple platforms and a broad set of processor instruction sets and executable formats.
summary.cons: The README includes a Security Warning noting that known security vulnerabilities exist within certain versions of Ghidra, so users are advised to review the Security Advisories before proceeding with installation or use.
summary.fit: Given its origin in NSA's cybersecurity mission and described use for analyzing malicious code, Ghidra appears best suited for software reverse engineering analysts and security researchers; advanced development work is noted to work best with Eclipse.

repos.name: anthropics / knowledge-work-plugins
repos.description: Open source repository of plugins primarily intended for knowledge workers to use in Claude Cowork

summary.goal: Knowledge Work Plugins packages skills, connectors, slash commands, and sub-agents into 11 role-specific plugins (e.g., sales, finance, legal, data) that aim to turn Claude into a specialist for a given job function, built for Claude Cowork and also compatible with Claude Code.
summary.usage: Cowork users install plugins from claude.com/plugins/. Claude Code users first run `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins`, then `claude plugin install sales@knowledge-work-plugins` (substituting the desired plugin); once installed, skills activate automatically and slash commands like `/sales:call-prep` become available.
summary.pros: Each plugin bundles domain skills that Claude draws on automatically, explicit slash commands, and MCP connectors to external tools; every component is file-based (markdown and JSON), requiring no code, infrastructure, or build steps.
summary.cons: The README describes these plugins as generic starting points that appear to become genuinely useful mainly after customization — editing `.mcp.json` for your tool stack and adding company-specific context to skill files — so out-of-the-box results may be limited until that setup is done.
summary.fit: Appears suited to teams or companies wanting to tailor Claude to their own tools, terminology, and processes across functions like sales, finance, legal, or data, using Claude Cowork or Claude Code.

repos.name: Tencent / WeKnora
repos.description: Open-source LLM knowledge platform: turn raw documents into a queryable RAG, an autonomous reasoning agent, and a self-maintaining Wiki.

summary.goal: WeKnora is described as an open-source, LLM-powered knowledge framework built for enterprise-grade document understanding, semantic retrieval, and autonomous reasoning, organized around RAG-based Quick Q&A, a ReAct Agent, and a Wiki Mode that turns raw documents into an interlinked markdown knowledge base.
summary.usage: Documented installation clones the repository (`git clone https://github.com/Tencent/WeKnora.git`), copies `.env.example` to `.env`, then runs `docker compose pull` followed by `docker compose up -d`; the Web UI is then reachable at `http://localhost`. Prerequisites listed are Docker, Docker Compose, and Git.
summary.pros: The architecture is documented as fully modular, with swappable LLMs, vector databases, and storage backends, supporting local or private-cloud deployment for full data sovereignty. It also lists 20+ LLM provider integrations and Langfuse-based observability.
summary.cons: The README's Security Notice states that login authentication was added starting v0.1.3 and recommends deploying in internal/private network environments rather than exposing the service directly to the public internet, suggesting that production-grade hardening is left as a manual operator responsibility.
summary.fit: Given its emphasis on self-hosted, modular document Q&A, multi-source data ingestion, and enterprise workspace RBAC, WeKnora appears best suited to organizations seeking an internally deployed knowledge/RAG platform rather than a lightweight public-facing tool.

repos.name: abue-ammar / tinycast
repos.description: Tinycast — a tiny, fully native macOS launcher, hotkeys, and clipboard history.

summary.goal: Tinycast is described as a fully native macOS launcher built with SwiftUI and AppKit using Swift 6.0, summoned by a global hotkey, and documented as using under 100 MB of RAM.
summary.usage: Installed via Homebrew: first run `brew tap abue-ammar/tinycast`, then `brew install --cask tinycast` (Apple silicon, macOS 26 or newer) or `brew install --cask tinycast-universal` (Intel, macOS 26). After installing, a global shortcut is set under Settings → General to summon the palette.
summary.pros: Documented features include app launching, clipboard history, a calculator, Quicklinks, Apple Shortcuts integration, Snippets, custom shell commands, window management with 34 Rectangle-style actions, and the ability to run existing Raycast extensions natively as SwiftUI. The README also states it has zero third-party dependencies and no telemetry.
summary.cons: The README specifies macOS 26 or later is required, which may exclude users on older macOS versions. DMG downloads from Releases are also self-signed and require manually clearing the quarantine flag (`xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Tinycast.app"`), an extra step not needed with the Homebrew install.
summary.fit: Tinycast appears suited to Apple silicon or Intel Mac users running macOS 26 or later who want a lightweight native launcher and may already use Raycast extensions; it is distributed free under the AGPL-3.0 license.

repos.name: cilium / cilium
repos.description: eBPF-based Networking, Security, and Observability

summary.goal: Cilium is a networking, observability, and security solution built on an eBPF-based dataplane. It provides a flat Layer 3 network across single or multiple clusters using native routing or overlay mode, and enforces identity-based security policies across L3-L7 that are decoupled from network addressing.
summary.usage: Cilium is deployed as a CNI plugin for Kubernetes clusters, following the installation guide linked from the 'Installing Cilium' section. Stable images are published, for example, as quay.io/cilium/cilium:v1.20.2, with documented maintained branches v1.20, v1.19, and v1.18.
summary.pros: eBPF-based distributed load balancing can fully replace kube-proxy; identity-based L3-L7 network policies support DNS- and HTTP-aware rules; Cluster Mesh enables multi-cluster connectivity; and built-in observability via Hubble integrates with Prometheus/Grafana.
summary.cons: Native routing mode requires the underlying network to be able to route application container IP addresses directly, which may limit deployment options depending on existing infrastructure. Additionally, only the last three minor Cilium versions receive maintained stable releases, with older versions considered EOL.
summary.fit: Cilium appears well suited for Kubernetes and multi-cluster environments needing eBPF-based networking, L7-aware security policy enforcement, and service mesh capabilities; images are distributed for AMD64 and AArch64 architectures.

repos.name: jamiepine / voicebox
repos.description: The open-source AI voice studio. Clone, dictate, create.

summary.goal: Voicebox is presented as a local-first, open-source AI voice studio that combines voice cloning and text-to-speech generation with dictation and speech-to-text, positioned as a free alternative to ElevenLabs and WisprFlow running entirely on the user's machine.
summary.usage: Users can download prebuilt installers for macOS and Windows, or run `docker compose up` for a Docker deployment. For local development, the README documents cloning the repo with `git clone https://github.com/jamiepine/voicebox.git`, then running `just setup` followed by `just dev` to start the backend and desktop app.
summary.pros: The README lists 7 TTS engines, support for 23 languages, zero-shot voice cloning, post-processing audio effects, an unlimited-length generation pipeline, and a built-in MCP server so agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Cline can speak in a cloned voice via a REST API.
summary.cons: Prebuilt Linux binaries are not yet available, so Linux users appear to need a build-from-source setup, which likely adds installation complexity compared to the packaged macOS and Windows options.
summary.fit: This suggests Voicebox may suit developers and privacy-conscious users who want a self-hosted voice I/O stack for dictation, TTS, and AI agent voice output, with its API-first and MCP design implying it is meant to be integrated into custom apps and agent workflows.

repos.name: affaan-m / ECC
repos.description: The agent harness performance optimization system. Skills, instincts, memory, security, and research-first development for Claude Code, Codex, Opencode, Cursor and beyond.

summary.goal: ECC is an open-source, MIT-licensed engineering system and toolbox for coding agents, built primarily for Claude Code, that adds a structured workflow (plan, test, implement, review, verify, remember, improve) around agent-generated code.
summary.usage: Install via the guided setup command `npx ecc-universal@2.2.1 setup`, or inside Claude Code run `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` followed by `/plugin install ecc@ecc`. The universal package requires Node.js 18+, and the Claude plugin path additionally requires Git and Claude Code 2.1 or newer.
summary.pros: The bundle includes 68 agents, 292 skills, and 94 legacy command shims, along with hooks, rules, memory, continuous learning, and AgentShield security scanning for auditing agent configurations.
summary.cons: Full feature parity is documented only for Claude Code; other harnesses such as Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, Zed, GitHub Copilot, Antigravity, and Qwen receive capability-limited adapters, so users should check the support status matrix rather than assume equivalent functionality.
summary.fit: ECC appears best suited to teams already standardized on Claude Code who want a repeatable engineering workflow and a security scanning layer; it may be less suitable for those needing full-parity support across many non-Claude harnesses.

repos.name: roboflow / supervision
repos.description: We write your reusable computer vision tools. 💜

summary.goal: Supervision is described in the README as a computer vision toolkit that supplies reusable building blocks, from data loading to real-time zone counting, so developers can focus on building applications around their own models.
summary.usage: Install with `pip install supervision` in a Python>=3.10 environment. The library connects to model outputs from libraries such as Ultralytics, Transformers, MMDetection, or Inference, or accepts detections directly from integrations like rfdetr, then applies annotators (e.g., BoxAnnotator) to visualize results.
summary.pros: It offers model-agnostic connectors so it can plug into many detection/classification/segmentation libraries, a wide range of customizable annotators for composing visualizations, and dataset utilities to load, split, merge, and save datasets in formats like YOLO, COCO, and Pascal VOC.
summary.cons: Some workflows depend on external services or extra packages: using the Inference connector appears to require a Roboflow API key, and certain examples need optional dependencies (e.g., `pip install pillow rfdetr`) installed separately, which suggests setup may vary by integration.
summary.fit: This appears best suited for developers who already have or plan to use a detection/classification/segmentation model and want a common layer for annotation and dataset handling rather than a standalone model.

repos.name: JustVugg / colibri
repos.description: Run frontier MoE models on hardware you already own — pure C, zero deps, experts streamed from disk. Tiny engine, immense model. 🐦

summary.goal: Colibrì is described as a C-based inference engine for running frontier Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models ranging from 744B to 2.8T parameters on consumer and heterogeneous hardware. It treats storage, RAM, and VRAM as a single multitier inference hierarchy, aiming to reduce hardware dependency and cost. Nine model families, including GLM-5.2, are documented as supported.
summary.usage: The README shows starting a chat session with `./coli chat`, and serving via `./coli web` or `./coli serve`. Installation options include downloading a prebuilt release and extracting it, or building from source with `git clone https://github.com/JustVugg/colibri && cd colibri/c` followed by `./setup.sh`, which requires gcc or clang with OpenMP.
summary.pros: The engine is documented to stream only actively routed experts using a JIT-like per-layer LRU cache and learned hot-store, avoiding the need to fit the entire model in fast memory. It supports dual-SSD striping for combined read bandwidth and reportedly ran a 744B model on hardware such as a 25 GB RAM laptop, without requiring a GPU.
summary.cons: Running the reference GLM-5.2 model requires about 372 GB of disk space for weights, and the README states there is no SLA on speed. Performance depends on available fast memory and drive characteristics, with O_DIRECT gains described as drive-dependent.
summary.fit: Based on the README's framing, this appears suited to users or researchers wanting to run very large MoE models on limited or heterogeneous local hardware rather than cloud APIs, and to contributors interested in inference-systems research.

repos.name: TencentCloud / Octop
repos.description: A smarter, self-hosted AI assistant — multi-user, multi-agent.

summary.goal: Octop is described as an open-source, self-hosted AI assistant with a multi-agent architecture intended for households, families, and small teams, aiming to keep conversations, workspaces, and credentials on the user's own machine.
summary.usage: Install with the one-line script `curl -fsSL https://finnie-1258344699.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/octop/install.sh | bash` (macOS/Linux; PyPI, Docker, and Windows installers are also documented), then initialize with `octop init` and start the service with `octop run`, after which the dashboard is reachable at http://127.0.0.1:8088.
summary.pros: The README lists built-in security controls (JWT multi-user isolation, tool approval, shell guardrails, PII redaction), a connector ecosystem with OAuth/MCP, and pluggable storage backends including local disk, Docker, PostgreSQL, and COS/S3.
summary.cons: Running the single process requires a modern multi-core CPU with a few GB of RAM plus sufficient disk space for the database, workspaces, and document corpora, which suggests it may not suit very low-resource environments; the roadmap is also explicitly noted as indicative and subject to change.
summary.fit: Given the self-hosted, single-process design and stated focus on households/small teams and per-user agent workspaces, Octop appears best suited to individuals or small groups wanting local control rather than large-scale enterprise deployments.

repos.name: cline / cline
repos.description: Autonomous coding agent as an SDK, IDE extension, or CLI assistant.

summary.goal: Cline is an open source coding agent that edits code, runs bash commands, and automates development workflows, available as a CLI, desktop app (macOS/Windows), VS Code extension, JetBrains plugin, and SDK for building custom agents.
summary.usage: Install the CLI with `npm i -g cline` or the SDK with `npm install @cline/sdk`; the CLI can run headless for scripting and CI/CD, schedule recurring agent runs with `cline schedule create`, and connect to chat platforms with commands like `cline connect telegram`. Documentation is hosted at https://docs.cline.bot.
summary.pros: It works with numerous model providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter with 200+ models, AWS Bedrock, Azure/GCP Vertex, Cerebras/Groq, Ollama/LM Studio, and OpenAI-compatible APIs), offers Plan/Act modes with human-in-the-loop approval or auto-approve, tracks edits with checkpoints for easy undo, and supports plugins, MCP servers, and multi-agent teams.
summary.cons: The JetBrains plugin is currently not open-sourced, unlike the CLI, SDK, and VS Code extension; the README also marks the VS Code extension's repository location as 'WIP migrating,' suggesting the project's code organization may still be in transition.
summary.fit: This project appears suited for developers seeking a model-agnostic coding agent embedded in their editor, terminal, or CI/CD pipeline, though teams specifically requiring an open-source JetBrains integration may find that piece currently unavailable.

repos.name: coder / coder
repos.description: Secure environments for developers and their agents

summary.goal: Coder is a self-hosted platform for cloud development environments and AI coding agents. Workspaces are defined with Terraform and connected through a Wireguard tunnel; Coder Agents executes an AI coding agent loop in the control plane rather than in workspaces.
summary.usage: On Linux/macOS, Coder can be installed with `curl -L https://coder.com/install.sh | sh`, or via a binary/installer from GitHub Releases on Windows. Running `coder server` starts the server at http://localhost:3000 to create the initial user, a Docker template, and a first workspace. For production, `coder server --postgres-url <url> --access-url <url>` adds a PostgreSQL database and external access URL.
summary.pros: Idle workspace resources shut down automatically to reduce costs, and the README states developers can be onboarded in seconds rather than days. Coder Agents can use models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Bedrock, or self-hosted providers without storing LLM credentials in workspaces, alongside centralized model governance, cost tracking, and audit logging.
summary.cons: A production deployment appears to require adding a PostgreSQL database (version 13 or later) and configuring an external access URL. Without these flags, Coder relies on a built-in database and a `*.try.coder.app` URL, which the README seems to frame as suited for evaluation rather than production use.
summary.fit: Coder appears suited to organizations wanting self-hosted, Terraform-defined cloud development environments across infrastructure like EC2, Kubernetes, or Docker, with governance over AI coding agents. A Premium tier with dedicated support and additional paid features is noted for large teams.

repos.name: n8n-io / n8n
repos.description: Fair-code workflow automation platform with native AI capabilities. Combine visual building with custom code, self-host or cloud, 400+ integrations.

summary.goal: n8n is a fair-code platform for building and deploying AI agents and workflow automation. It combines a visual canvas with custom code, can run self-hosted or in the cloud, and connects to 1500+ integrations, supporting multi-step AI workflows from prototype to production.
summary.usage: Quick start uses an install script that requires Docker: `curl -fsSL https://get.n8n.io | sh`. Alternatively, deploy manually with `docker volume create n8n_data` followed by `docker run -it --rm --name n8n -p 5678:5678 -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n`, then access the editor at http://localhost:5678.
summary.pros: n8n offers model flexibility across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and open-source providers without changing architecture, supports JavaScript, Python, and npm packages for custom logic, and includes 1500+ integrations plus 9,000+ workflow templates to connect existing systems.
summary.cons: n8n is distributed under the Sustainable Use License and a separate n8n Enterprise License rather than a standard open-source license, and additional enterprise features and support require contacting license@n8n.io, which may mean added licensing considerations for teams needing those capabilities.
summary.fit: n8n appears best suited for teams needing self-hosted or cloud AI automation with enterprise controls such as role-based access and audit trails, though the quick-start path assumes Docker is already available.

repos.name: ayghri / i-have-adhd
repos.description: A skill to stop your coding agent from burying the answer. ADHD-friendly output.

summary.goal: i-have-adhd is a skill/plugin for coding assistants intended to make responses action-first, with numbered steps and no filler phrases like "Hope this helps!" (README lines 34-38).
summary.usage: Install by pasting a CLI prompt referencing https://github.com/ayghri/i-have-adhd and the repo's AGENTS.md (lines 26-29), or follow INSTALL.md (line 32). To customize, fork the repo, edit skills/i-have-adhd/SKILL.md, then run commands such as `claude plugin uninstall i-have-adhd`, `claude plugin marketplace add <your-username>/i-have-adhd`, and `claude plugin install i-have-adhd@i-have-adhd` (lines 86-93).
summary.pros: It defines 10 explicit rules, such as leading with the next action, numbering multi-step tasks, and capping lists to 5 items, which appear intended to reduce verbose or meandering assistant replies (lines 69-82).
summary.cons: Customizing the skill requires forking and manually removing the upstream plugin/marketplace entry first, since the fork and upstream share the same name, an operational step documented as a prerequisite for tuning (lines 86-93).
summary.fit: It appears suited for developers using coding assistants who want concise, action-oriented output; the README notes it is ADHD-friendly without requiring an ADHD diagnosis and is loosely adapted from an ADHD self-help book for LLM responses rather than human routines (lines 5, 99).

repos.name: bilawalsidhu / gods-eye-view
repos.description: A spy satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real. Live open source spatial intelligence on a photorealistic 3D globe.

summary.goal: God's Eye View is an open-source, browser-based 3D globe application that visualizes public live data feeds—including aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic, and public cameras—alongside hands-free voice control powered by a realtime AI agent.
summary.usage: It can be installed via Pinokio with one click, or run locally by cloning the repository and running `git clone https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git`, `npm ci`, `npm run doctor`, and `npm run dev`, then opening http://localhost:4173. Optional API keys (Cesium ion, Google Maps, OpenAI) can be added afterward through the app's POWER UP panel to unlock photorealistic 3D and voice features.
summary.pros: The app starts without any API keys, using Esri satellite imagery and keyless terrain by default, with flights, satellites, earthquakes, and public cameras available out of the box. It is released under the MIT License, runs locally, and its data layers are structured as separate modules that can be extended.
summary.cons: Photorealistic 3D and voice features require additional provider keys (Cesium ion, Google Maps, OpenAI) subject to each provider's terms, quotas, and metered billing. Some data, such as simulated traffic, camera pose estimates, and rocket trajectories, is approximated rather than directly observed, and a documented cold-start benchmark (1.86s) is described as a one-time comparison rather than a guaranteed result.
summary.fit: Based on its MIT license and description as 'an evolving open-source client for exploration and learning' rather than a hardened production service, the project appears best suited to developers, hobbyists, and researchers exploring geospatial visualization and OSINT/GEOINT concepts—not for safety-critical navigation or operational decisions, which the README explicitly discourages.

repos.name: mksglu / context-mode
repos.description: Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and   enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks.

summary.goal: Context Mode is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server built for AI coding agents. Its documented goal is reducing how much raw tool output — such as file reads, web fetches, and command results — enters the model's context window, while also preserving session state such as edited files and pending tasks across conversation compaction.
summary.usage: Claude Code users install it as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode` followed by `/plugin install context-mode@context-mode`, then restart Claude Code and run the diagnostics command to confirm the install. The documented prerequisite for this plugin path is Claude Code v1.0.33+; other supported clients register the same server as an MCP tool provider instead.
summary.pros: The README states that raw command output is processed inside an isolated sandbox subprocess, so only relevant results reach the conversation, with one documented example of a 315 KB session output reduced to about 5.4 KB — roughly a 98% reduction. It also documents no telemetry and no required account, since session data stays local.
summary.cons: On platforms without hook support, such as the Antigravity IDE and Zed, the README states that routing enforcement depends on a manually copied instruction file rather than automatic interception, and estimates this reaches only about 60% of the context savings achieved with hooks. The Cursor plugin is also documented as still awaiting marketplace review.
summary.fit: Based on the company logos presented as users, Context Mode appears suited to both individual developers and engineering teams working across MCP-compatible AI coding clients — the README documents support for 17 such clients plus an OpenClaw gateway integration. It is released under the Elastic License 2.0, a source-available license disallowing hosted or managed-service offerings.

repos.name: openai / plugins
repos.description: OpenAI Plugins

summary.goal: This repository provides a curated collection of example plugins for Codex, demonstrating how developers can build plugin bundles for tools such as Figma, Notion, SwiftUI-based iOS/macOS apps, web apps, Expo, Netlify, Remotion, and Google Slides.
summary.usage: Each plugin is organized under plugins/<name>/ and must include a .codex-plugin/plugin.json manifest, with optional companion files like skills/, .app.json, .mcp.json, agents/, commands/, hooks.json, and assets/. The default marketplace configuration is located at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json, pointing to the plugins/ directory.
summary.pros: The repository offers several richer, real-world examples spanning design (Figma), knowledge work (Notion), mobile/desktop development (build-ios-apps, build-macos-apps, expo), and web deployment (build-web-apps, netlify), giving developers multiple reference implementations for learning plugin structure.
summary.cons: Users authenticating with an API key appear to rely on a separate marketplace file (.agents/plugins/api_marketplace.json) rather than the default one, which suggests the plugin discovery setup may differ depending on login method and could require additional configuration awareness.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited for developers already working within the Codex ecosystem who want reference examples for building or extending plugins across design, productivity, and app-development domains, rather than for those seeking a single standalone tool.

repos.name: max-sixty / worktrunk
repos.description: Worktrunk is a CLI for Git worktree management, designed for parallel AI agent workflows

summary.goal: Worktrunk is a command-line tool for managing git worktrees, built for running multiple AI coding agents (such as Claude Code and Codex) in parallel. It provides three core commands intended to make working with worktrees as straightforward as working with branches.
summary.usage: Worktrunk can be installed via Homebrew with `brew install worktrunk && wt config shell install`, or via Cargo with `cargo install worktrunk && wt config shell install` (Windows, Arch Linux, and Conda/Pixi installs are also documented). A typical workflow starts a worktree with `wt switch --create feature-auth`, then inspects worktrees with `wt list`.
summary.pros: The README documents features such as hooks for automating setup at various workflow stages, LLM-generated commit messages, a merge workflow that squashes and rebases in one command, an interactive picker with diff/log previews, shared build caches across worktrees, and PR checkout support.
summary.cons: Shell integration must be explicitly installed via `wt config shell install` for commands to change directories, and on Windows the `wt` command name conflicts with Windows Terminal's own command, requiring installation as `git-wt` instead unless that alias is disabled.
summary.fit: Worktrunk appears best suited for developers who run several AI coding agents in parallel using git worktrees and want a CLI to reduce the manual steps git worktree normally requires; it documents support for macOS, Linux, Windows, and Arch Linux.

repos.name: obra / superpowers
repos.description: An agentic skills framework & software development methodology that works.

summary.goal: Superpowers is described as a complete software development methodology for coding agents, built on composable skills paired with initial instructions that ensure the agent invokes them automatically.
summary.usage: Installation of Superpowers is harness-specific; for Claude Code, run `/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official` from the official marketplace, or register a separate marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace` followed by `/plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace`. Once installed, skills like brainstorming, writing-plans, and test-driven-development activate automatically to guide design, planning, and RED-GREEN-REFACTOR implementation.
summary.pros: The skills library covers testing, debugging, collaboration, and meta workflows, and the documented basic workflow emphasizes test-first development, code review between tasks, and evidence-based verification before completion. It supports multiple coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI, among other supported harnesses.
summary.cons: Because installation differs by harness, using Superpowers with more than one coding agent requires installing it separately for each, which could add setup and update overhead.
summary.fit: This methodology appears best suited to teams already working with one of the supported coding agents who want a structured, mandatory design-to-implementation workflow, and may be less fitting for those seeking a lightweight, optional process.

repos.name: blader / humanizer
repos.description: Agent skill that removes signs of AI-generated writing from text

summary.goal: Humanizer is a Markdown-based skill that rewrites AI-sounding text so it reads as if written by a person, without changing what the text says. According to the README, it works with any agent that supports skills.
summary.usage: Install it with the Skills CLI using `npx skills add blader/humanizer --global` for a global install, or omit `--global` for a project-only install; the skill responds to `/humanizer`. On Claude Code 2.1.142 or newer, it can instead be installed as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer` and `/plugin install humanizer@humanizer`, responding to `/humanizer:humanizer`. Claude Desktop requires a manual install by downloading the repo as a ZIP or copying SKILL.md into the agent's skill folder.
summary.pros: The rewrite process shows its work: an initial draft, a short critique, and a final version. It edits only prose, leaving code, data, frontmatter, and link targets unchanged, and the README states it does not invent facts, asking for missing details instead. It also supports voice matching from a writing sample, and organizes its checks into 25 numbered patterns ordered by strength and frequency.
summary.cons: Several patterns are documented as 'weak alone,' meaning they justify an edit only when multiple tells appear together in a passage, since a careful writer may use any one deliberately; this suggests some rewrite decisions may need human judgment in ambiguous cases.
summary.fit: This tool appears suited to users of skill-supporting agents such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop who want a documented, pattern-based way to reduce AI-sounding phrasing while preserving factual content; the README does not indicate support for agents lacking skills capability.

repos.name: microsoft / markitdown
repos.description: Python tool for converting files and office documents to Markdown.

summary.goal: MarkItDown is a lightweight Python utility for converting files such as PDF, PowerPoint, Word, Excel, images, audio, HTML, CSV/JSON/XML, ZIP archives, YouTube URLs, and EPubs into Markdown, intended for use with LLMs and related text analysis pipelines.
summary.usage: Install with `pip install 'markitdown[all]'` and convert a file from the command line using `markitdown path-to-file.pdf > document.md`. A Python API is also documented via `from markitdown import MarkItDown`, along with optional Azure Document Intelligence or Content Understanding endpoint configuration for cloud-based conversion.
summary.pros: The documentation describes support for many file formats, optional dependency groups (e.g. `[pdf]`, `[docx]`, `[pptx]`) for installing only what's needed, and support for 3rd-party plugins such as `markitdown-ocr` that extend functionality without modifying the core repository.
summary.cons: The README's Security Considerations section states that MarkItDown performs I/O with the privileges of the current process, similar to `open()` or `requests.get()`, and advises sanitizing inputs and calling narrower `convert_*` functions in untrusted environments, implying that unrestricted use with untrusted input could carry risk.
summary.fit: The project is documented as a Python library meant to be incorporated into other systems rather than an end-user application; the contribution scope explicitly excludes web servers, REST/HTTP APIs, hosted conversion services, and desktop/mobile applications, suggesting it fits backend or pipeline integration better than standalone deployment.

repos.name: home-assistant / core
repos.description: :house_with_garden: Open source home automation that puts local control and privacy first.

summary.goal: Home Assistant is an open source home automation platform that prioritizes local control and privacy. It is developed by a worldwide community of tinkerers and DIY enthusiasts and is designed to run on hardware such as a Raspberry Pi or a local server.
summary.usage: The README points to home-assistant.io for a live demo, installation instructions, tutorials, and full documentation. Users experiencing issues during setup or component development are directed to the Home Assistant help section on the same site.
summary.pros: The platform uses a modular architecture that makes it straightforward to add support for new devices or actions, with documented guidance for creating custom components. It also benefits from community development and backing from the Open Home Foundation.
summary.cons: The README itself does not include self-contained installation steps; setup, architecture, and component-creation details are all documented externally, so users likely need to consult the linked home-assistant.io resources rather than this file alone to get started.
summary.fit: Given its emphasis on local control, privacy, and self-hosting on devices like a Raspberry Pi, Home Assistant appears best suited to DIY users and hobbyists managing their own smart-home setups rather than those seeking a fully managed cloud service.

repos.name: kunchenguid / firstmate
repos.description: Talk to one agent. Ship with a crew.

summary.goal: firstmate is presented as an "agent distro" — a portable directory of instructions, skills, tooling, and state conventions — that lets a single primary coding agent (the "first mate") dispatch and supervise a crew of autonomous "crewmate" agents to complete parallel software tasks such as fixes, investigations, plans, and audits, delivering finished pull requests, approved local merges, or standalone investigation reports.
summary.usage: Setup begins with `gh auth login`, then `git clone https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate` and `cd firstmate`, followed by launching a supported harness inside the cloned repo, such as `claude` (Claude Code) or `grok --trust` (Grok); AGENTS.md then governs the session. Documented requirements include Git, the GitHub CLI, and a verified primary harness, with tmux as the reference runtime backend.
summary.pros: The first mate acts as a single liaison to a visible crew running in tmux windows, herdr tabs, or other backend sessions, and each task reportedly runs in its own disposable git worktree so parallel work on one repo never collides. Supervision is described as event-driven and zero-token, waking the first mate only when needed, and state is said to be restart-proof, persisting on disk so a killed session can be reconciled and resumed.
summary.cons: Some functionality depends on harness-specific setup steps: Grok reportedly needs `--trust` once per clone for its hooks and turn-end guard to load, and Cursor Agent CLI is noted to have no turn-end hook in headless mode, so its primary session must run interactively. The README also states that `codex-app` is not yet a supported runtime backend, and it separately labels the Zellij and Orca backends as experimental.
summary.fit: Based on the documented feature set, firstmate appears best suited to developers already using one of the listed harnesses (Claude Code, Grok, Pi, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor Agent CLI) who want to run several agent-driven tasks in parallel across isolated git worktrees rather than manually juggling terminal sessions; the README is explicit that firstmate itself is not a model, harness, or CLI, but an overlay distro layered on top of one.

repos.name: petergyang / no-ai-slop
repos.description: Removes 20+ patterns of AI slop from any piece of writing.

summary.goal: No AI Slop is a skill for removing more than 20 documented patterns of "AI slop" writing—such as binary contrasts ("It's not X. It's Y."), throat-clearing openers, and fake-profound endings—while aiming to preserve the writer's personal voice.
summary.usage: Install it by pasting "Install the /no-ai-slop skill globally from https://github.com/petergyang/no-ai-slop" into ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent, or by running npx skills add petergyang/no-ai-slop --skill no-ai-slop --global --yes. Then invoke /no-ai-slop (your writing) to edit text, or /no-ai-slop is this slop? (your writing) to detect slop patterns.
summary.pros: The README states the editing mode preserves personal voice and lists what it changed, while the detection mode quotes every slop pattern found. It also checks writing fundamentals such as leading with the point, active voice, and concrete detail over abstraction.
summary.cons: The detection mode explicitly quotes slop patterns "without guessing whether AI wrote the text," so it likely cannot confirm authorship, only flag matching phrasing patterns.
summary.fit: Given its install path, it appears best suited to people already working inside ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or similar coding-agent environments to review or generate writing.

repos.name: danny-avila / LibreChat
repos.description: Enhanced ChatGPT Clone: Features Agents, MCP, Skills, DeepSeek, Anthropic, AWS, OpenAI, Responses API, Azure, Groq, o1, GPT-5, Mistral, OpenRouter, Vertex AI, Gemini, Artifacts, AI model switching, message search, Code Interpreter, langchain, DALL-E-3, OpenAPI Actions, Functions, Secure Multi-User Auth, Presets, open-source for self-hosting. Active

summary.goal: LibreChat is a self-hosted, open-source AI chat platform (currently at v0.8.8-rc3) that unifies multiple AI providers — including Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Google, and AWS Bedrock — into one privacy-focused interface, while adding features like AI Agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) support, Code Interpreter, and Artifacts.
summary.usage: It can be deployed via one-click templates for Railway, Zeabur, or Sealos, or self-hosted using its bundled Docker Compose stack described as a one-command setup; full setup and configuration documentation is hosted at docs.librechat.ai.
summary.pros: It supports numerous AI providers plus custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints without requiring a proxy, includes multi-user authentication (OAuth2, LDAP, email login) with a browser-based admin panel for managing users, groups, and roles without redeploying, and provides resumable streams that reconnect across tabs and devices.
summary.cons: The README explicitly instructs users to review the changelog for breaking changes before updating, implying upgrades between versions can introduce compatibility changes. Several newer capabilities, such as attached code workspaces and Agent Plugins, are labeled beta or 'highly experimental,' so they may not yet be stable enough for production use.
summary.fit: Because it is self-hosted and open-source, LibreChat appears best suited for individuals or organizations that want direct control over their AI infrastructure and data privacy rather than relying solely on a vendor-hosted chat interface.

repos.name: stablyai / orca
repos.description: Orca is the ADE for working with a fleet of parallel agents. Run any coding agent with your own subscription. Available on desktop, mobile and remote runtime.

summary.goal: Orca is presented as an AI orchestrator that runs multiple coding-agent CLIs — including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Pi — side by side, each in its own isolated git worktree, tracked from a single interface (lines 19-20).
summary.usage: Orca is a desktop app installable by downloading from onOrca.dev, or via package managers: `brew install --cask stablyai/orca/orca` on macOS, or `yay -S stably-orca-bin` on Arch Linux. An accompanying CLI supports scripted workflows such as `orca worktree create`, and `orca serve` runs it on headless Linux servers.
summary.pros: It supports macOS, Windows, and Linux, and works with any CLI agent that runs in a terminal. Listed capabilities include parallel worktrees for fanning one prompt across multiple agents, SSH worktrees for remote execution, and a mobile companion app for monitoring and steering agents remotely.
summary.cons: The README states its feature list is 'perpetually behind' because updates ship daily, suggesting documentation may not always reflect the latest capabilities. Headless Linux server use is also noted as needing a separate setup guide, implying extra configuration beyond the desktop install.
summary.fit: Based on these details, Orca appears best suited to developers who want to coordinate multiple AI coding agents in parallel across isolated worktrees, including remote SSH environments, rather than users seeking a single lightweight agent tool.

repos.name: Panniantong / Agent-Reach
repos.description: Give your AI agent eyes to see the entire internet. Read & search Twitter, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, XiaoHongShu — one CLI, zero API fees.

summary.goal: Agent Reach is an open-source capability layer that gives AI coding agents (such as Claude Code, OpenClaw, Cursor, or Windsurf) the ability to fetch and read content from platforms like YouTube, GitHub, Twitter/X, Reddit, Bilibili, and RSS feeds, by selecting, installing, and health-checking backend connectors for each platform rather than implementing the reading itself.
summary.usage: To install, a user copies a single instruction containing the URL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/agent-reach/main/docs/install.md and gives it to their AI agent, which then runs the setup. The CLI also provides commands such as agent-reach doctor to check per-platform connector status and agent-reach install --system for explicit, user-approved system-level installation.
summary.pros: The project describes itself as fully open-source and free, storing cookies only on the local machine. It uses a preferred-plus-fallback backend routing model per platform (for example, switching from yt-dlp to bili-cli when one is blocked) and includes the agent-reach doctor command for diagnosing connector status. It is documented to work with any command-line-capable agent.
summary.cons: Platforms requiring login, such as Twitter/X, Xiaohongshu, Reddit, Facebook, and Instagram, need cookies or an existing browser session, and the README recommends using a dedicated secondary account, since scripted access on such cookies is described as carrying a risk of account suspension. Reddit is noted as having no zero-configuration path because anonymous access is blocked.
summary.fit: This tool appears suited to developers who already run command-line-driven AI agents locally or on a server and want broad, multi-platform read access without building scrapers themselves. OpenClaw users must first enable exec permission (tools.profile set to "coding") for the agent to run shell commands, which the README lists as a prerequisite specific to that platform.

repos.name: decolua / 9router
repos.description: Unlimited FREE AI coding. Connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Cline, Copilot, Antigravity to FREE Claude/GPT/Gemini via 40+ providers. Auto-fallback, RTK -40% tokens, never hit limits.

summary.goal: 9Router is a free, open-source local router that aims to connect AI coding CLI tools such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, and OpenClaw to 40+ AI providers and 100+ models through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, to reduce token usage and avoid per-provider rate limits.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npm install -g 9router`, then run `9router` to open the dashboard at http://localhost:20128. Connect a provider (e.g., a free option) from the dashboard, then point a CLI tool's OpenAI-compatible endpoint to http://localhost:20128/v1 with the generated API key. Docker images are also published.
summary.pros: The built-in RTK token saver reportedly compresses tool outputs to cut 20-40% of input tokens per request. A three-tier fallback (subscription → cheap → free) is designed to avoid downtime when quota runs out. Multi-account routing and compatibility with many CLI tools and 40+ providers are also described.
summary.cons: Some free-tier providers have documented limits and changes: Kiro AI's free tier has been capped at 50 credits/month since September 2025, and the iFlow, Qwen Code, and Gemini CLI free tiers were discontinued in 2026, so free routing options are not guaranteed to remain stable long-term. Running from source requires Node.js 20+.
summary.fit: 9Router appears best suited for developers already using a supported CLI coding tool who want to consolidate multiple AI provider accounts and reduce token spend, though teams needing precise real-time billing may need to treat its dashboard cost figures as estimates only.

repos.name: tt-a1i / archify
repos.description: Agent skill for beautiful, verifiable architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, and lifecycle diagrams—self-contained HTML with motion and crisp export.

summary.goal: Archify is a Node.js rendering and validation system for Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenCode that turns a codebase or system description into a polished, interactive system map directly in chat, using typed JSON IR compiled deterministically into HTML/SVG.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npx skills add tt-a1i/archify -g`, then describe a system in agent chat with no repository required. The bundled CLI also supports commands such as `node archify/bin/archify.mjs compare architecture base.json head.json architecture-delta.html --json` for comparing architecture snapshots before merge.
summary.pros: It offers five diagram types and four presets with dark/light themes, produces a self-contained HTML file plus PNG, SVG, WebM, and 1200×630 share-card exports, and runs atomic schema, layout, and route validation before delivering output.
summary.cons: The README states that automatic Mermaid parsing, general-purpose auto-layout, hosted sharing, and WYSIWYG editing are intentionally outside current scope, so teams needing those capabilities may find the tool insufficient on its own.
summary.fit: This appears best suited to teams already using Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, or OpenCode who want agent-generated, validated architecture diagrams rather than a general-purpose drawing editor; the current development version is v2.17.0-dev.1, released under the MIT license.

repos.name: omacom / omarchy
repos.description: Beautiful, Modern & Opinionated Linux

summary.goal: Omarchy is presented as a Linux distribution created by DHH, described as "beautiful, fun & agentic," with more information available at https://omarchy.org.
summary.usage: Its documentation is organized in a manual/ directory, also mirrored at https://learn.omacom.io/2/the-omarchy-manual, covering topics such as Getting Started, Hotkeys, and the Omarchy CLI; since no separate installation command is given, setup and navigation appear to begin with the "Getting Started" and "Coming From Mac or Windows" manual pages.
summary.pros: It is released under the MIT License (https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT), and its manual spans roughly fifty pages covering applications, configuration, theming, hardware, security, and troubleshooting topics.
summary.cons: Because documentation is split across dozens of separate manual files rather than one consolidated guide, users may need to check multiple pages to piece together full setup or configuration details, and cross-platform users may need to rely on the separate "Windows VM" and "Mac support" pages, suggesting native support is Linux-centric.
summary.fit: Omarchy appears best suited to Linux users wanting a preconfigured desktop environment with built-in AI, development, and theming tools, though platform or hardware prerequisites beyond the listed manual topics are not specified.

repos.name: anthropics / claude-plugins-community
repos.description: Community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. Read-only mirror — submit plugins at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission.

summary.goal: Claude Plugins — Community is documented as a read-only mirror of the community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. The .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file lists plugins available for installation, synced nightly from Anthropic's internal review pipeline.
summary.usage: Plugins can be installed from claude.com/plugins/ for Claude Cowork, or through the Claude Code CLI, which requires first adding the marketplace and then installing a specific plugin by running `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community` followed by `claude plugin install <plugin-name>@claude-community`.
summary.pros: Every listed plugin has passed automated security scanning and been approved for distribution before appearing in the marketplace. Submissions go through a single, centralized intake point at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission rather than ad hoc channels.
summary.cons: Because the marketplace list syncs only nightly from an internal pipeline, the visible plugin set may lag behind the actual review state by up to a day; exact update timing and discrepancy handling are not detailed in the source material.
summary.fit: This repository appears suited for users who want to browse and install pre-vetted plugins through the documented web interface or CLI, rather than contribute code directly, since pull requests opened against the repo are closed automatically.

repos.name: cursor / plugins
repos.description: Cursor plugin specification and official plugins

Each plugin lives in its own standalone directory at the repository root, defined by a `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest, and covers categories such as Developer Tools, Productivity, and Integrations.
